extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readership and readers interested in 19th-century marriage/divorce law and public policy
extracted.subtask_short: debate on marriage and divorce law
extracted.subtask_description: Printed letters and commentary debating what legally and morally constitutes Marriage and what grounds and procedures divorce law should recognize; includes a verbatim excerpt of the Indiana divorce statute (as of March 1, 1860).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Marriage (lexicographic/Christian standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is 'a union and consecration of one man to one woman for life' (standard lexicographers and the Christian Church), and other unions are denied the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace Greeley cites standard dictionaries and the Christian Church as the authoritative definitions; he insists the term 'Marriage' should be held to that meaning alone and that unions terminable at will do not qualify as 'Marriage' under this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency requirement for filing divorce (Indiana §6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorces may be decreed by the Circuit Courts on petition filed by any person who has been a bona fide resident of the State one year prior to filing and a resident of the county at the time of filing; such bona fide residence must be proven to the satisfaction of the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural prerequisite: petitioner must prove residency to the court's satisfaction before divorce can be decreed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Adultery (Indiana §7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adultery is a ground upon which divorces shall be decreed upon application of the injured party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute lists adultery first among specified grounds but adds 'except as hereinafter provided' (see exceptions in §8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Impotency (Indiana §7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impotency is a statutory ground for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an explicit cause in the statute authorizing divorce decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Abandonment for one year (Indiana §7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment of one party by the other for one year is a statutory ground for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute specifies a one-year abandonment period as qualifying cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Cruel treatment (Indiana §7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cruel treatment of either party by the other is a statutory ground for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute authorizes divorce where cruelty is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Habitual drunkenness or failure to provide (Indiana §7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual drunkenness of either party, or the failure of the husband to make reasonable provision for his family, is a statutory ground for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause couples habitual intoxication and inadequate support as bases for divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Conviction of infamous crime after marriage (Indiana §7.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conviction, subsequent to the marriage, in any country, of either party of an infamous crime is a statutory ground for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal conviction post-marriage of an infamous crime qualifies as cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for divorce — Other causes at Court's discretion (Indiana §7.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any other cause for which the Court shall deem it proper that a divorce should be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch-all provision authorizing the court to grant divorce for other causes it deems proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adultery exception — Connivance (Indiana §8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorces shall not be granted for adultery when the offence has been committed with the connivance of the party seeking the divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petitioner connived at the adultery, adultery cannot be relied upon as ground for divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adultery exception — Voluntary cohabitation or delay in filing (Indiana §8.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorces shall not be granted for adultery when the party seeking the divorce has voluntarily cohabited with the other, with knowledge of the fact; or has failed to file their petition for two years after discovering the adultery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute bars relief where the injured party condoned the adultery by living with the adulterer or delayed more than two years in bringing the petition after discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adultery exception — Mutual guilt (Indiana §8.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorces shall not be granted for adultery when the party seeking the divorce has also been guilty of adultery under such circumstances as would have entitled the opposite party, if innocent, to a divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual or comparable fault by the petitioner disqualifies adultery as a ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court duty regarding minor children (Indiana §21)
rubrics_metrics.description: In decreeing a divorce the Court shall make provision for the guardianship, custody, support, and education of the minor children of such marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement that the court address children's guardianship, custody, maintenance and education when granting divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of divorce — full dissolution (Indiana §23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The divorce of one party shall fully dissolve the marriage contract as to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute declares that a divorce decree dissolves the marital contract for both parties (i.e., complete dissolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of out-of-state divorces (Indiana §24)
rubrics_metrics.description: A divorce decreed in any other State by a court having jurisdiction thereof shall have full effect in this State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full faith/credit style provision: divorces validly decreed elsewhere are effective in Indiana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of prosecuting attorney on undefended petitions (Indiana §27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever a petition for divorce remains undefended, it shall be the duty of the prosecuting attorney to appear and resist such petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute imposes a public-duty safeguard to contest undefended divorce petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No limited divorce permitted (statutory note)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indiana law (as printed) does not permit limited divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The printed note explicitly states that limited (i.e., divorce from bed and board or partial separations) is not allowed under the Indiana statute as provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture — divorces decreed upon application of the injured party
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorces shall be decreed upon the application of the injured party (statutory framing of §7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute contemplates the injured spouse bringing the petition; combined with residency and proof requirements this frames who may initiate proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative standard (Robert Dale Owen) — divorce justified when union defeats its sacred ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorce is justified and may become a duty when a long train of abuses and immoralities shows a union has become destructive of its holy ends; 'when it becomes the daily source of anger, strife, cruelty, brutality, it ... becomes itself immoral, and ought to cease.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen argues from moral and scriptural grounds that divorce laws admitting multiple causes are defensible when marriage no longer serves higher moral purposes; he also emphasizes children’s welfare and that trivial causes should not dissolve unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative standard (Horace Greeley) — limited ground (adultery) and deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Only adultery (as affirmed by Jesus, in Greeley's reading) should be the ground for divorce; divorce should authorize (not require) legal dissolution of obligations for the innocent party; indissoluble marriage deters frivolous/unfit marriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley frames divorce policy as a moral deterrent: making marriage harder to dissolve prevents heedless or appetite-driven unions and preserves society's standards.
